current_answer: NVIDIA Research reports a warm Sol-H3 T2VA path on eight B300s: nominal 5/10/15-second 1344×768 outputs with audio took 1.653/3.732/6.612 seconds through text encoding, four-forward denoising, and VAE decoding. Loading, warmup, and final MP4 encoding were excluded. NVIDIA lists continuous 24-fps delivery and in-session interaction as future work. This is a fast inference route, not a verified live service. Vidu S2-Editing adds a hosted live-feed editing route to the existing H3 clip, session, and queue routes: its documentation specifies an incoming RTC video feed, edited RTC output, optional RTMP relay, and in-session reference changes. It is not text-to-video or an independently verified continuous public show. At one credit per billed second and the listed $0.005 standard credit, editing alone implies $18 per billed hour before delivery costs. The source gives no independent control-to-viewer delay, long-session reliability, or cost invoice. Current evidence supports several distinct routes: fal H3 Max Director is a finite hosted context-carrying WebRTC session; Yoroll says H3 Superfast powers YoLive, a group proposal-and-vote route; Reactor FastH3 is a high-end queue-and-playout route; FastVideo documents local FastH3 clip paths and a four-GPU Dreamverse frame-carried Preview v1 profile; a community project reports one RTX 5090 sustaining a retimed dense FastH3 channel; Comfy offers local H3 paths; and vLLM-Omni documents a separate H3 service. vLLM-Omni’s current H3 recipe says step execution can admit requests between denoise steps, but its stated two-H100 test found four simultaneous H3 jobs slower under four-way co-batching than ordinary request mode. Its documented two-RTX-5090 DLO launch selects the FL2VA task path, which serves T2VA and FL2VA, and recommends a 384 GiB host; its one 50-step T2VA validation returned about 5.17 seconds of output in 8 minutes 38 seconds. Treat task path, client capability, arrival pattern, and a recorded output as separate facts. No cited H3 result establishes a live viewer experience. Comfy Org also reports that its H3 VAE encode/decode round trip fell from 24.3 to 12.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 at 1344×768, 129 frames after the v0.36.0 update; this is a VAE-stage A/B, not a full-render or live-speed result. vLLM-Omni v0.30.0 now documents opt-in Ref2VA long-video latent-tail continuation; its maintainer reports one 30.667-second, 736-frame H3 result on eight B300 GPUs. This is a completed-output route with no published full wall time, cost, first frame, or live playout result. A separate current vLLM-Omni FastH3 Dense eight-B300 T2VA test returned 4.4 seconds of output in 11.7-11.8 seconds after warmup: four denoiser evaluations took about 2.36-2.37 seconds, but the complete response remained slower than playback. Turbo adapter choice is task- and artifact-specific; a four-step label is not an end-to-end speed or live guarantee.

catalogue_card.question: Five seconds of H3 in 1.653 seconds—can it run a live show?
catalogue_card.text: NVIDIA reports that warm Sol-H3 timing on eight B300s, but it excludes final MP4 encoding. Continuous delivery and in-session control remain future work. Read the setup before treating the speed as a stream.

summary: NVIDIA Sol-H3 reports eight-B300 warm medians of 1.653/3.732/6.612 seconds for nominal 5/10/15-second 1344×768 T2VA outputs with audio. Final MP4 encoding, load, and compilation are excluded; continuous streaming and in-session control remain future work. The 11.04× five-second comparison also changes Base H3 from 49 denoiser forwards to a four-forward FastH3 adapter.

Vidu S2-Editing documents a source-fed live editing path: publish video into RTC, subscribe to edited RTC output, and optionally relay it to RTMP. It bills one credit per live second; at a $0.005 standard credit, 3,600 billed seconds imply $18 before delivery costs. No independent viewer-delay or long-session result is available.

vLLM-Omni’s current recipe reports a separate warmed eight-B300 FastH3 Dense T2VA test: a 4.4-second, 1344×768 clip returned as a complete MP4 in 11.7 and 11.8 seconds. Four denoiser evaluations took 2.36–2.37 seconds, so the complete short-clip response was still slower than playback. This is distinct from the previously reported longer FastH3 profile that beat its playback clock.

vLLM-Omni v0.30.0 documents opt-in Ref2VA long-video continuation. Its maintainer reports one 736-frame, 30.667-second original-H3 output on eight B300 GPUs at 1344×768, 24 fps, 50 steps; full wall time and live delivery are not supplied.

Comfy Org reports that the H3 video VAE encode/decode round trip fell from 24.3 to 12.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 at 1344×768, 129 frames after its v0.36.0 update. This is one stage, not whole-job speed.

vLLM-Omni says H3 can admit and retire requests between denoise steps, but its stated two-H100 test with four simultaneous 672×384, 209-frame, 30-step requests reports worse wall time and mean latency under four-way co-batching than ordinary request mode.
The source says staggered-arrival behavior remains unmeasured. The benchmark does not predict two RTX 5090 GPUs, a different job shape, a FastH3 adapter, a browser-visible result, or a public stream.

The current two-RTX-5090 DLO launch selects the FL2VA DiT; T2VA uses that path. The source recommends a 384 GiB host, while its one 50-step T2VA validation returned 124 1344×768 / 24 fps frames in 8 minutes 38 seconds.
vLLM-Omni’s current ComfyUI client still accepts one FL2VA frame even though the server recipe can represent ordered first-and-last-frame inputs.
uncertainty: Sol-H3 results are project-reported, not pool-tested; final encoded-to-viewer time, quality acceptance, queue behavior, session reliability and cost are unknown.
Vidu S2 Editing topology and billing are provider-documented; no pool or independent timed RTC-to-RTMP session, billed invoice, viewer latency, or long-run reliability record was found.

The new FastH3 Dense timing is two project-reported warm runs on eight B300 GPUs for one 4.4-second T2VA shape; no pool reproduction, cost, video-quality, queue, first-frame, or viewer result is available.
The vLLM-Omni long-video example is a project-maintained eight-B300 result. The 300-second request cap does not validate five-minute output, acceptable joins, cost, or a stream.

The ComfyUI VAE speed figures are provider-maintained node-level A/B measurements on one RTX 5090 setup. Full H3 render time, quality under a pinned workflow, repeated-run reliability, and cost impact remain unmeasured.
The batching result is one project-maintained two-H100 benchmark with four simultaneous requests. Staggered arrivals, other job shapes, other hardware, and viewer-visible behavior remain unmeasured.
The documented two-RTX-5090 result is one project-published T2VA validation. The pool did not independently audit its environment, media, timing, or quality.

The two-5090 command selects the FL2VA path; it does not establish a combined multi-task service, Ref2VA, a two-keyframe client workflow, warm performance, streaming, queueing, or first visible frame.
vLLM-Omni’s current ComfyUI client-scope statements come from an open RFC. The pool did not install or test the server or client.
Dreamverse’s FastH3 profile is project documentation; the pool did not install or run it, inspect a generated handoff, or measure buffer, cost, recovery, or uptime.
FastVideo and ComfyUI still conflict on FastH3 8-Step V2 FL2VA scope. The pool did not run a pinned T2VA or FL2VA workflow.
No pool test, invoice, uptime log, end-to-end source-to-visible latency measurement, or first-party pool analytics record is available.
freshness_note: Checked 1 October 2026. Sol-H3 adds a fast eight-B300 warm inference route, not a measured live session or delivered-hour cost.
